Why Should South Africans Care about Brexit?

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The United Kingdom, within Europe, is a major importer of South African goods, but after Brexit, what will become of our trade agreements with the British?

Unique Selling Point:
For those South African companies with European headquarters in the UK, how much harm will Brexit do to their business, when it blocks their convenient gateway to the continent?

Summary:
The deadline for the UKs exit from Europe is fast approaching - 29th March 2019. The UK was split down the middle in the referendum, the British government is now battling to get a deal agreed to by its members of parliament. The country has woken up to the myriad of consequences that simple vote in 2016 has invoked. Europe has long been aware of the far reaching ramifications of the UK's exit plan, but now as the moment of truth gets closer the rest of the world is paying much more attention to what it means for them. With almost a fifth of South African exports going to the UK and our historical links with the country, it's about time South Africa got to grips with what Brexit means... for us.


Further information:
Lord Peter Hain, a former South African who after exile forged a successful career as a British politician, in the Labour Party, is well equipped to illuminate the topic for our viewers. He is a firm anti-Brexiteer especially given:
- the xenophobic roots of the Brexit movement,
- Peter's central involvement as Secretary of State for Northern Ireland in the Northern Ireland peace process, which Brexit is threatening to destabilize,
- and for the impact on trade of the UK's departure from the EU.
Peter forms part of the central narrative of the story.

Douglas Gibson, a former opposition chief whip in the South African parliament is a self-professed positive thinker. He has highlighted positive opportunities for South Africa in light of Brexit... to fill the gap in trade links that Britain will lose with the EU. We interview Douglas to find out what opportunities he thinks are in this for South Africans. South Africa is the third biggest trading partner for the UK in the Commonwealth and trade between the two countries has increased in the last 10 years. Will Brexit, with the weakening of British links to Europe, mean we can grow our trade with the United Kingdom even more?

Rob Davies the Minister of the DTI is the person who has to deal with the trade fall-out of Brexit on behalf of South African commerce. His work load is growing, with the onset of negotiating new trade agreements with the UK. With the possibility of a 'no deal' Brexit looming how can South Africa ensure the growth in trade with the UK continues to our mutual benefit?

The economist Goolam Balim believes that Brexit is disastrous for the South African economy and for neighbouring countries too. He has conducted research on the impact on Southern African businesses.

Mr. Rob Davies
Mr. Goolam Ballim Economist

Press Release:


Brexit: What It Means for South Africa
The end of March deadline for Britain’s withdrawal from the European Union is fast approaching and the interminable and bruising internal debates will give way to real-world impact. About 5% of South African exports go to the United Kingdom and it’s also a major tourist destination so what ramifications will the looming Brexit bring? We analyse how a more insular, weaker Britain might spell hard times for Britain’s trading partners.
Producer: Sophia Phirippides
Presenter: Derek Watts and John Webb
Researcher: Tony Beamish


Script:


House of Commons 15-01-19 Biggest Defeat for May Deal.

Speaker: Order Order….

VO: Everyone is in agreement about one thing, Brexit, the process of the United Kingdom leaving the European Union is in need of order.

[House_of_Commons_15-01-19_19-37-39 Biggest Defeat for May Deal.mov] 00:01:33 )

Sound up: Murmur murmur… “ The nos to the left 432”

VO: Chaos reigned in January this year, when the Prime Minister of the UK, Theresa May, was handed the biggest defeat in a parliamentary vote since the 1920’s. Her Brexit deal with the EU was rejected by a thumping majority.

[House_of_Commons_15-01-19_19-37-39 Biggest Defeat for May Deal.mov] 00:01:39

Sound up Speaker….the ayes to the right 202, the nos to … order! The ayes to the right 202, the nos to the left 432, so the nos have it, the nos have it. Unlock!!!

VO: In 2016, The UK was virtually split down the middle in a referendum, that went in favour of Brexit. But now, on the home stretch Britain has woken up to the myriad of consequences that a simple vote has invoked.

Sound up.. Independence Day

Peter: I think Brexit is more serious for Britain than anything else that we've faced since the run up to the war against Hitler.

LINK JOHN & DEREK: The deadline for Brexit is almost here. At 11pm on the 29th of March, 2019, the United Kingdom it seems, will be leaving the European Union after over 40 years of being part of the European Community.//

[President Tusk 29 March 2017 Announcing UK invoke article 50.mov] 00:00:06
Sound up: So here it is, 6 pages, the notification from Prime Minister Theresa May triggering article 50, and formally starting the negotiations of the United Kingdom’s withdrawal from the European Union.

LINK JOHN: What does this mean for the United Kingdom

LINK DEREK: and what impact will it have on South Africa?

VO: Economist Goolam Ballim says Brexit will not be without challenges for the UK and South Africa.

Goolam: Britain straddles sometimes between fourth and fifth in terms of the league table in trading partners, it takes in about 5% of South Africa’s exports. It’s a significant trading partner and of course if it shrinks as a market it’s going to hurt South African exports.

VO: Opinions vary about Brexit’s impact on its trading partners, but Theresa May is resolved on what her deal will deliver for the British people.

[Theresa May 25 Nov 2018 European Council Brussels.mov]

Theresa May: First control of our borders not an emergency break on free movement or a promise of greater transition controls in the future but an end to the free movement of people in full once and for all.

Peter: I think Brexit is more serious for Britain than anything else that we've faced since the run up to the war against Hitler.

VO: Lord Peter Hain, a former South African who after his parent’s exile, forged a successful career as a British politician, in the Labour Party, is a firm anti-Brexiteer especially given, what he argues are the xenophobic roots of the Brexit movement.

Peter: It has ignited a far right project that is operating across the world, Trump in America and the Brexiteers are aligned, so you've seen Islamophobic attacks increase, racist attacks increase and anti Semitic attacks increase as the right feels it has legitimacy because of the referendum results in 2016.

VO: Globalisation has been good for countries like China and India where poverty has fallen overall, but in countries like Britain and America the middle classes have stagnated.

Peter: There used to be a situation where you were better off than your parents and your parents were better off than their parents. Thats gone into reverse for all except a minority

Derek: The Brexiteers talk about getting back control. What does that mean

Peter: Globalization exists on a massive basis, the integration of the financial and trading economies of the world means you don’t get back control by leaving a large organization, you actually lose influence.

VO: Although Theresa May originally campaigned to stay in the EU, now with Brexit an almost done deal, she wants to ensure that Britain is not left behind, especially with Europe as a leading player within the global economy.

[Theresa May 25 Nov 2018 European Council Brussels.mov] [00:02:57]

Theresa May: But I have been just as determined that as well as taking back control this should be a deal that protects the things we value in our relationship with our European friends and sets us on course for a future of opportunity and prosperity.

Peter: To break links with a market where half our trade is done in goods and services seems to me to be lunacy
It’s the largest, richest single market in the world. 500 million people

Derek: We talk about a deal or no deal Brexit its like a gameshow with huge ramifications.

Peter: Theresa May's deal doesn’t resolve anything because the future trading relationship that Britain wants to enjoy with the EU is left open and to be negotiated [01:09:13.14] and could take years after the end of March.

Derek: With a no deal exit the UK could be left in a legal economic and political limbo?

Peter: We would suddenly fall out of long standing trading relationships, an open border through the channel tunnel, an open border across the island of Ireland, all those advantages would suddenly stop and the consequences will be catastrophic.

VO: And to show how open the border really is, John took a short trip over the border between Northern Ireland in the UK, and the Republic of Ireland

John: This then is the great Irish border crossing we’re in the UK and we’re now in the republic of Ireland…

JOHN LINK: It’s not much to look at, but this stretch of land is central to the Brexit negotiations. And at its core, is something known as “the backstop”

VO: The backstop is a safety net, to guarantee an open border between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, in case the UK leaves the EU without a comprehensive deal in place. So no deal means no “backstop”.

Peter: The Irish border has been open for decades, it’s got millions of goods crossing it every year.

LINK JOHN: So why is a hard border such a big issue? Well, apart from the economic impact and its effect on trade between Northern Ireland and the Republic, there is also a psychological impact. It’ll be a very physical reminder of a painful past.

Peter: The Irish border which is invisible now and a very important part of the peace process in northern Ireland will become a hard border if we just fall out and that will ignite a lot of the old anger and tensions, the achilles heel of a hardline Brexit.

VO: Allround a no deal brexit means that long standing agreements with the EU will have to be renegotiated from scratch. But even a negotiated Brexit will pose its own problems.

LINK JOHN: The Brexit negotiations have been confusing, if not downright chaotic and you feel the impact of that in Dublin. Barclays Bank has relocated a significant portion of its business from the UK to the Irish capital. And when I say significant, I mean assets worth 250 Billion Euros.

Peter: Honda cars are only this week in Swinden employing 3500 people has already said it’s going to close. Jaguar Land Rovers already locating one of its new vehicles to Slovakia I see Brexit as igniting a with draw of a lot of crucial foreign investment right across the economy.

LINK JOHN: So, how much harm will Brexit do to South African companies with their European headquarters in the UK? When that convenient gateway to Europe suddenly closes and they may have to relocate?

Goolam: Several South African firms have got real estate interests they also have retail interests in the British market. And we’ve already seen several firms on the stock exchange have been marked down, because of the prospects of lower demand out of the United Kingdom.

LINK Derek: Negotiating new trade agreements takes time with complicated changes in policy and a no deal Brexit could mean going back to the drawing board for South Africa

VO: And nobody know this better than Dr Rob Davies, Minister of Trade and Industry.

Rob: If we have a disorderly interruption in our trade then companies involved in export trading with the UK that’s in the auto sector in wine, various fruit products, there would be some interruption and some disruption, unless we're able to smooth over this transition.

VO: South Africa got in early with its post Brexit negotiations and should there be a hard or no deal Brexit there are bilateral agreements that will fall into place.

Rob: We are working to iron out the last issues so that we can hopefully get this ratified by our parliament before it rises towards the end of next month

VO: Brexit is not only about trade it’s also about the movement of people, and some South Africans may be concerned about travel and accessibility to the UK and Europe.

Goolam: many south Africans do have British passports as a function of ancestry and that in turn has allowed them quite a flexible entry for work and visiting to the European Union, this could come under siege.

VO: But for the British, the Brexit endgame could threaten the UK’s very future as a union.

Peter: It’s likely that Scotland will have another referendum and could leave the UK in order to stay in the EU. It’s also likely that there could be a border pole in Northern Ireland in order for Northern Ireland to join with the republic of Ireland as is provided by the peace process. Both those dangers are more real as a result of Brexit.

Peter: We would suddenly fall out of long standing trading relationships, an open border through the channel tunnel, an open border across the island of Ireland, all those advantages would suddenly stop and the consequences will be catastrophic. VO: And to show how open the border really is, John took a short trip over the border between Northern Ireland in the UK, and the Republic of Ireland John: This then is the great Irish border crossing we’re in the UK and we’re now in the republic of Ireland… JOHN LINK: It’s not much to look at, but this stretch of land is central to the Brexit negotiations. And at its core, is something known as “the backstop” VO: The backstop is a safety net, to guarantee an open border between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, in case the UK leaves the EU without a comprehensive deal in place. So no deal means no “backstop”. Peter: The Irish border has been open for decades, it’s got millions of goods crossing it every year. LINK JOHN: So why is a hard border such a big issue? Well, apart from the economic impact and its effect on trade between Northern Ireland and the Republic, there is also a psychological impact. It’ll be a very physical reminder of a painful past. Peter: The Irish border which is invisible now and a very important part of the peace process in northern Ireland will become a hard border if we just fall out and that will ignite a lot of the old anger and tensions, the achilles heel of a hardline Brexit. VO: Allround a no deal brexit means that long standing agreements with the EU will have to be renegotiated from scratch. But even a negotiated Brexit will pose its own problems. LINK JOHN: The Brexit negotiations have been confusing, if not downright chaotic and you feel the impact of that in Dublin. Barclays Bank has relocated a significant portion of its business from the UK to the Irish capital. And when I say significant, I mean assets worth 250 Billion Euros. Peter: Honda cars are only this week in Swinden employing 3500 people has already said it’s going to close. Jaguar Land Rovers already locating one of its new vehicles to Slovakia I see Brexit as igniting a with draw of a lot of crucial foreign investment right across the economy. LINK JOHN: So, how much harm will Brexit do to South African companies with their European headquarters in the UK? When that convenient gateway to Europe suddenly closes and they may have to relocate? Goolam: Several South African firms have got real estate interests they also have retail interests in the British market. And we’ve already seen several firms on the stock exchange have been marked down, because of the prospects of lower demand out of the United Kingdom. LINK Derek: Negotiating new trade agreements takes time with complicated changes in policy and a no deal Brexit could mean going back to the drawing board for South Africa VO: And nobody know this better than Dr Rob Davies, Minister of Trade and Industry. Rob: If we have a disorderly interruption in our trade then companies involved in export trading with the UK that’s in the auto sector in wine, various fruit products, there would be some interruption and some disruption, unless we're able to smooth over this transition. VO: South Africa got in early with its post Brexit negotiations and should there be a hard or no deal Brexit there are bilateral agreements that will fall into place. Rob: We are working to iron out the last issues so that we can hopefully get this ratified by our parliament before it rises towards the end of next month VO: Brexit is not only about trade it’s also about the movement of people, and some South Africans may be concerned about travel and accessibility to the UK and Europe. Goolam: many south Africans do have British passports as a function of ancestry and that in turn has allowed them quite a flexible entry for work and visiting to the European Union, this could come under siege. VO: But for the British, the Brexit endgame could threaten the UK’s very future as a union. Peter: It’s likely that Scotland will have another referendum and could leave the UK in order to stay in the EU. It’s also likely that there could be a border pole in Northern Ireland in order for Northern Ireland to join with the republic of Ireland as is provided by the peace process. Both those dangers are more real as a result of Brexit.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The United Kingdom, within Europe, is a major importer of South African goods, but after Brexit, what will become of our trade agreements with the British?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: For those South African companies with European headquarters in the UK, how much harm will Brexit do to their business, when it blocks their convenient gateway to the continent?
metadata.Summary: The deadline for the UKs exit from Europe is fast approaching - 29th March 2019. The UK was split down the middle in the referendum, the British government is now battling to get a deal agreed to by its members of parliament. The country has woken up to the myriad of consequences that simple vote in 2016 has invoked. Europe has long been aware of the far reaching ramifications of the UK's exit plan, but now as the moment of truth gets closer the rest of the world is paying much more attention to what it means for them. With almost a fifth of South African exports going to the UK and our historical links with the country, it's about time South Africa got to grips with what Brexit means... for us.
metadata.Further information: Lord Peter Hain, a former South African who after exile forged a successful career as a British politician, in the Labour Party, is well equipped to illuminate the topic for our viewers. He is a firm anti-Brexiteer especially given: - the xenophobic roots of the Brexit movement, - Peter's central involvement as Secretary of State for Northern Ireland in the Northern Ireland peace process, which Brexit is threatening to destabilize, - and for the impact on trade of the UK's departure from the EU. Peter forms part of the central narrative of the story. Douglas Gibson, a former opposition chief whip in the South African parliament is a self-professed positive thinker. He has highlighted positive opportunities for South Africa in light of Brexit... to fill the gap in trade links that Britain will lose with the EU. We interview Douglas to find out what opportunities he thinks are in this for South Africans. South Africa is the third biggest trading partner for the UK in the Commonwealth and trade between the two countries has increased in the last 10 years. Will Brexit, with the weakening of British links to Europe, mean we can grow our trade with the United Kingdom even more? Rob Davies the Minister of the DTI is the person who has to deal with the trade fall-out of Brexit on behalf of South African commerce. His work load is growing, with the onset of negotiating new trade agreements with the UK. With the possibility of a 'no deal' Brexit looming how can South Africa ensure the growth in trade with the UK continues to our mutual benefit? The economist Goolam Balim believes that Brexit is disastrous for the South African economy and for neighbouring countries too. He has conducted research on the impact on Southern African businesses.
